sections.body: Selective attention can be framed as a family of gating mechanisms that improve behavior by prioritizing relevant inputs and suppressing distracting ones. The alpha-oscillation source emphasizes neural suppression of irrelevant sensory processing, while the mindfulness source distinguishes behavioral attention subsystems that can change with training.
sections.title: Shared Concept

sections.body: Alpha-band evidence supports an active-suppression account: alpha power rises in cortical regions processing irrelevant visual, auditory, tactile, spatial, feature-based, or intersensory information. Stronger naturally occurring or induced alpha is linked to reduced visual cortical excitability and weaker perceptual detection.
sections.title: Alpha-Band Suppression

sections.body: Mindfulness evidence provides a behavioral counterpart rather than a direct neural mechanism. The Attention Network Test separates alerting, orienting, and conflict monitoring, and the reported effects differ by training history: MBSR improves endogenous orienting, while intensive retreat experience alters alerting-related readiness.
sections.title: Mindfulness and Attention Subsystems

sections.body: The cross-source synthesis is strongest at the level of attention as selective control. The available evidence does not show that mindfulness training causes alpha-band suppression changes, so the relationship should be treated as conceptual rather than causal.
sections.title: Synthesis Boundary

sections.body: Across the sources, cortical organization matters both for conscious experience and for selective attention, but the claims operate at different explanatory levels. Information integration theory addresses the conditions for conscious experience, while alpha-band attention research addresses suppressive modulation of sensory processing.
sections.title: Shared Concept

sections.body: Information integration theory argues that consciousness depends on complexes with high integrated information. A distributed thalamocortical network is presented as well suited for consciousness because it combines functional specialization with functional integration.
sections.title: Integrated Conscious Systems

sections.body: Alpha-band attention research describes suppressive modulation as primarily cortico-cortical, involving frontal and parietal networks, with possible thalamo-cortical contributions when distracting sensory processing must be reduced. Higher alpha is linked to lower visual excitability and weaker detection.
sections.title: Attention Networks and Alpha Control

sections.body: A cautious synthesis is that conscious access and attentional suppression both depend on organized interactions among specialized cortical systems. The provided evidence does not establish alpha oscillations as a direct measure of integrated information or consciousness.
sections.title: Synthesis Boundary
